source.version: Journal version of record: Research in Engineering Design (2026) 37:34, doi 10.1007/s00163-026-00497-x; received 3 April 2026, revised 30 June 2026, accepted 13 July 2026, published online 31 August 2026 (p. 1). The journal header labels it 'REVIEW ARTICLE', but the paper reports an original experiment.
source.title_on_document: Human or model? A four-factor experimental study of design experience and image-generation alignment strategies in industrial product ideation

supplement.holds: No supplementary material or online appendix is identified in the 19-page journal PDF, which contains the main article and references; no appendix or embedded supplementary file is included. The recorded descriptive and inferential statistics are in Tables 3 to 7 (pp. 9, 11, 12, 14, 15) and Fig. 5 (p. 13). The document's silence does not establish that no separate supplement exists. Data availability states: 'No datasets were generated or analysed during the current study.' (p. 17)

paper_design_summary: Sixty participants from the authors' affiliated universities were analyzed in a laboratory experiment: each completed four 10-minute motorcycle concept-design tasks using Midjourney V6 or ChatGPT-4o image generation crossed with concrete or abstract prompts, with order set by a balanced Latin square and no stated random allocation to sequences. Design experience and AIGC tool proficiency were measured and used to classify participants into six groups; all four task conditions used generative AI (pp. 5-7; Fig. 3, p. 10). Two blind senior product-design experts rated each participant's selected image per condition for quality and novelty and coded its attributes for an image-level creative diversity score, while participants self-reported perceived usefulness (pp. 7-9).

studies.label: Lab experiment: motorcycle concept design with Midjourney V6 vs ChatGPT-4o image generation and concrete vs abstract prompts (3 x 2 x 2 x 2 mixed design)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Within person: every participant completed all four conditions (image generator Midjourney V6 = IGAS0 or ChatGPT-4o = IGAS1, crossed with concrete PT0 or abstract PT1 prompts), and the order of the four tasks was set by a 4 x 4 balanced Latin square. The paper never says participants were randomly allocated to sequences. The between-subjects factors (design experience, AIGC tool proficiency) were not assigned: participants were classified into groups from a pre-test questionnaire. No condition without AI exists.
assignment.quote: To control for order effects, task sequences were assigned using a 4 × 4 balanced Latin square design.
assignment.locator: p. 7, Sect. 3.3 (Latin square); p. 6, Sect. 3.2.2 (within-subjects factors); p. 5, Sect. 3.1 (groups classified from the pre-test questionnaire)

participants.exclusions: No exclusions or attrition reported. Sixty people were recruited, 10 in each experience-by-proficiency group (p. 5, Sect. 3.1), and 60 people were analyzed: Fig. 3 shows submitted images from all 60 participants in all four conditions (p. 10), consistent with the repeated-measures ANOVA error df of 54 in Tables 4 to 6 (pp. 11, 12, 14). Each condition contains the same 60 people. The 20 images excluded from the formal dataset were rater-training images, not excluded participants (p. 7, Sect. 3.4). Random allocation to task sequences is not stated, so n_randomized remains null.
participants.who: 60 analyzed participants in six groups of 10 (design experience none/basic/advanced x AIGC tool proficiency low/high), classified from a pre-test questionnaire and verified academic backgrounds. No experience (EXP1): non-design majors with less than one year of training and no experience leading design projects; basic (EXP2): one to three years of systematic design training and limited project participation as team members; advanced (EXP3): more than three years of professional design education or practical experience and leadership of at least two complete projects. Low proficiency (ATP0): never used AIGC tools or under 1 h per week, under 3 months cumulative; high (ATP1): over 1 h per week for over 6 months (p. 5, Sect. 3.1). The acknowledgements thank 'experimental participants from our affiliated universities' (p. 17). Student or professional status is not stated, so population is null.

ai_tool.name_model: Midjourney V6 (aesthetic-prioritised alignment, IGAS0) and ChatGPT-4o image generation (instruction-following alignment, IGAS1), both accessed March 2025
ai_tool.how_used: In each 10-minute task, participants typed prompts of the assigned type (concrete or abstract) into the assigned image generator, generated and numbered as many motorcycle concepts as possible, and then selected one representative image to submit for that condition. Midjourney ran at default resolution, random seeds, and style about 750; ChatGPT-4o used a new chat window per task. Researchers pre-configured all settings, and a 5-minute procedural video preceded the tasks (p. 6). A post-hoc check found that the prompts behind the submitted images met the assigned prompt type (p. 7).

task.description: Motorcycle concept design: generate as many innovative motorcycle design concepts as possible with the assigned image generator and prompt type, then submit one representative image per condition.
task.duration: 10 minutes per task, four tasks with about 5 minutes of rest between tasks, in one lab visit that began with a 5-minute instructional video (pp. 6-7)

outcomes.name: Creative quality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two senior product-design experts (each over 7 years of combined industry practice and design teaching), trained on 20 practice images and blind to group and condition, rated five 5-point items: functional completeness, aesthetic/formal quality, technical feasibility, user orientation, overall completeness (Table 2, p. 8). Score = mean of the two experts; Cronbach alpha 0.847; ICC(3,2) = 0.703, 95% CI [0.664, 0.737] (p. 9). The paper calls quality 'the overall merit of a generated design concept' (p. 7); the construct is coded usefulness because the items rate the quality and feasibility of one output. One representative image per participant per condition (four per participant; the total image count is not printed). Four-factor mixed repeated-measures ANOVA with participant as subject (error df 54) and Holm-Bonferroni post hoc tests (SPSS 27.0).

outcomes.name: Creative diversity (image-level attribute variety score)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Despite its name, this is not diversity across people. Both experts coded each submitted image into categories on four attributes (form/structure, material and surface, conceptual style, ergonomics; Tables 1 and 2, p. 8). The finalised labels give an image-level 'attribute creative diversity score': the equal-weighted average of four attribute-level variety measures V1 to V4, range 0 to 1, following Shah et al. (2003). The formula is announced but not printed (p. 8). The paper states that 'the unit of classification and analysis was the individual submitted image, rather than a set of generated images or an image pool' (p. 8). Coded category_count because the score is computed from hand-coded categories, not rated. Analysed with an Aligned Rank Transform factorial ANOVA because scores were non-normal (Shapiro-Wilk p < .05), with Tukey-adjusted ART contrasts.

company_involvement.description: No company involvement stated. The tools are commercial products (Midjourney V6, ChatGPT-4o). Funding: 'The author declares no financial support.' Competing interests: 'The authors declare no competing interests.'

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 unclear: every participant completed all four generative-AI conditions (p. 6, Sect. 3.2.2), and task sequences were assigned using a balanced Latin square (p. 7, Sect. 3.3). The paper does not state that participants were randomly allocated to sequences; 'random' refers only to Midjourney seed values (p. 6, Sect. 3.2.3). The codebook requires randomized order for a within-person design. The two image generators and two prompt types provide ai_design contrasts under codebook sections 3 and 5; a no-AI arm is not required, and conventional treatment/control labels do not prevent eligibility. Design experience and AIGC proficiency were measured grouping factors (p. 5, Sect. 3.1). S1 is coded other because a randomized design class is not yet supported. Criterion 2 met: 60 people were analyzed, above the 50-person threshold; the recruitment count and groups are stated in Sect. 3.1 (p. 5), Fig. 3 shows outputs from all 60 in all four conditions (p. 10), and Tables 4 to 6 report error df 54 (pp. 11, 12, 14). No participant exclusions are reported. Criterion 3 met: two blind experts scored participants' prompted and selected images for quality and novelty (p. 7, Sects. 3.3-3.4; p. 8, Table 2; p. 9, Sect. 4). Perceived usefulness is self-report and does not supply eligibility; the image-level attribute diversity score is not diversity across people (p. 8, Sect. 3.4.4; p. 16, Sect. 5). Context class remains none while allocation is unresolved; this is an experiment in which people used AI, not an AI-versus-human output comparison. Core eligibility remains unclear pending author clarification of allocation to Latin-square sequences.

one_line_finding: With all 60 participants using generative AI in every condition, blind experts rated the submitted images higher with Midjourney V6 than with ChatGPT-4o image generation for creative quality (3.58 vs 3.11; difference 0.469, SE 0.107, p < .001) and novelty (3.12 vs 2.68; difference 0.444, SE 0.141, p = .003), and concrete prompts beat abstract prompts on quality only (difference 0.236, SE 0.104, p = .028) (Table 3, p. 9; Table 5, p. 12; Table 6, p. 14).
open_questions: Were participants randomly allocated to the Latin-square task sequences, and how was participant-to-sequence allocation implemented (p. 7, Sect. 3.3)? Author clarification is needed; this is the sole unresolved eligibility issue (criterion 1).

Were Table 3 SDs calculated over individual image scores pooled across conditions or over participant means (p. 9)? Authors should identify the aggregation and denominator before effect standardization; this does not change the three eligibility criteria.

What are the exact coding and calculation rules for the four attribute-level measures underlying the image-level creative diversity score? Sect. 3.4.4 describes an equal-weighted average but does not print the formula (p. 8). Authors could supply it; quality and novelty ratings already satisfy criterion 3, and pp. 8 and 16 settle that this is not diversity across people.

What were participants' student or professional statuses? The paper mentions non-design majors and participants from affiliated universities but does not identify the whole sample as students (p. 5, Sect. 3.1; p. 17, Acknowledgements). Authors could clarify the population code; this does not affect eligibility.
notes: Table 3 reports marginal factor-level means and SDs without per-level sample sizes or an explicit SD aggregation rule. The same 60 analyzed participants completed each AI condition (pp. 5-7; Fig. 3, p. 10); 'arm_means_sds_ns' uses these participant counts established from the study design, not separately printed Table 3 counts. Whether SDs describe image scores or participant means remains unresolved. Text-versus-table discrepancies: creative-quality PT0 mean 3.46 in the text (p. 11) vs 3.47 in Table 3 (p. 9); perceived-usefulness SDs in the text (p. 9: 0.66 and 0.83 for IGAS0 and IGAS1; 0.64 and 0.83 for PT0 and PT1) vs Table 3 (0.68, 0.86, 0.68, 0.82); novelty IGAS difference 0.44 in the text vs 0.444 in Table 6; diversity PT F 0.21 in the text vs 0.209 in Table 7. Tables 1 and 2 label the material categories differently (Steel; Alloy vs Steel/Metal-retro; Alloy/Plastic-modern). The paper names all four dependent variables as primary (p. 5), so every outcome is paper_primary and the label does not single one out. Partial eta squared is the paper's only effect size; no standardized mean difference is printed. Measured-group results, not coded as contrasts because design experience (EXP) and AIGC tool proficiency (ATP) were classified, not assigned: creative quality ATP0 3.34 (0.88) vs ATP1 3.35 (0.84), F(1, 54) = 0.005, p = .945, and EXP F(2, 54) = 0.172, p = .842 (Tables 3 and 5); novelty ATP1 3.11 (1.02) vs ATP0 2.71 (1.07), F(1, 54) = 7.778, p = .007, partial eta squared = .126, ATP1 > ATP0 mean diff 0.394, SE 0.141, 95% CI [0.111, 0.677], p_adj = 0.007, and EXP F(2, 54) = 0.079, p = .924 (Tables 3 and 6); creative diversity ATP0 0.38 (0.12) vs ATP1 0.38 (0.11), F(1, 162) = 0.07, p = .794 in the text, ART contrast t(54) = 0.26, p_adj = 0.794, and EXP F(2, 162) = 0.79, p = .459 (Sect. 4.5, Table 7); perceived usefulness shows EXP x IGAS F(2, 54) = 4.432, p = .017 and EXP x PT x ATP F(2, 54) = 4.496, p = .016 (Table 4). For creative diversity, the text reports the between-subjects EXP and ATP effects with 162 denominator df, while Table 7 reports their contrasts with t(54) (pp. 14-15). The paper does not supply ART model syntax; these reported degrees of freedom alone do not establish its error structure. The title's 'Human or model?' does not signal an AI-versus-human output comparison; no AI-only outputs are compared with human outputs. Data availability: 'No datasets were generated or analysed during the current study' (p. 17). An a priori G*Power analysis gave a minimum sample of about 54 (p. 5). Final review: S1 is coded other, a supervised within-person experiment with unreported sequence randomization (pp. 5-7); this supersedes the lab_rct assertion in the preserved reconciliation object. Generator and prompt-type comparisons qualify as ai_design under codebook sections 3 and 5. Neither tool or prompt type is designated a default, so treatment labels (Midjourney V6 and abstract prompts) are coding conventions; the reported strings retain the paper's IGAS0-minus-IGAS1 and PT0-minus-PT1 directions. Source.supplement.exists is not_stated because the document does not identify supplementary material; it does not establish its absence. Population is null because the paper does not establish that all participants were students. The final challenge counters count dispositions of checker problems, not the separate source/spec clarifications or open items. All reconciliation differences were already resolved, and the reconciliation object is retained unchanged.

challenge_resolution.problem: studies[S1].design_class (also the reconciliation.agreed_fields_checked entry for design_class, marked confirmed: true): lab_rct asserts randomization that the source does not establish.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: Changed studies[S1].design_class from lab_rct to other and clarified the design summary, eligibility reason, and notes. The Latin square establishes counterbalancing but does not establish random allocation to its sequences; measured experience and proficiency groups do not supply randomized AI assignment. assignment.randomized remains not_stated and criterion 1/core remain unclear. The old design_class confirmation in reconciliation is superseded by this final decision; reconciliation itself is unchanged as required.

challenge_resolution.locator: p. 7, Sect. 3.3; p. 6, Sects. 3.2.2-3.2.3 and Fig. 1; p. 5, Sect. 3.1; codebook sections 3-4; form-spec design_class field note

open_items.item: Random allocation to Latin-square task sequences remains unreported (p. 7, Sect. 3.3). Authors must explain participant-to-sequence allocation; this alone keeps criterion 1 and core eligibility unclear.

Resolved: comparisons of the two image generators or prompt types are ai_design contrasts under codebook sections 3 and 5 (pp. 6-7, Sects. 3.2.3-3.3). Neither alternative needs to be a no-AI arm. No default is designated, so treatment/control labels are conventions with the source contrast directions preserved; this adds no eligibility uncertainty.

Table 3 does not specify whether SDs describe individual image scores or participant means (p. 9). Authors should supply the aggregation rule and denominator for standardization; this does not alter criteria 1-3.

Resolved: participants generated concepts by prompting and selected the scored images, which experts rated (p. 7, Sects. 3.3-3.4; p. 8, Table 2; p. 9, Sect. 4). These are qualifying AI-assisted outputs for criterion 3. The generator's contribution limits interpretation as unaided human skill but requires no further eligibility evidence.

The creative diversity formula and precise attribute-level scoring rules are not printed (p. 8, Sect. 3.4.4); authors could supply them. The source already settles that this is variety within one submitted image, not across people (pp. 8, 16), and quality/novelty ratings independently meet criterion 3.

Student or professional status for the full sample is not stated; population is null pending author clarification (p. 5, Sect. 3.1; p. 17, Acknowledgements). Non-design majors and affiliated-university recruitment do not establish that everyone was a student. This does not affect the confirmed 60-person count or any eligibility criterion.

ART model syntax and repeated-measures error structure are not specified; Sect. 4.5 and Table 7 report different denominator degrees of freedom for between-person tests and contrasts (pp. 14-15). Authors could clarify precision for later pooling; this does not change eligibility.
